KEY MESSAGE 1... 

An active pattern will remain in place through the 
weekend due to broad WNW mid/upper flow across the Great Lakes 
between a broad trough over south central Canada and a broad ridge 
over the Desert Southwest and southern Plains. Multiple weak 
mid/upper shortwaves and associated surface waves emanating out of 
the broad trough will progress through the WNW flow and interact 
with a wavering quasi-stationary frontal boundary between the Ohio 
Valley and southern Great Lakes. This will support periods of 
convection given a seasonably warm and moist environment that will 
remain in place.

Starting off this morning, one weak mid/upper shortwave is 
progressing slowly east across northern Ohio. RAP analysis shows a 
weak surface reflection beneath an area of upper diffluence and mid-
level PVA, and this is encouraging broad isentropic ascent and 
focusing warm air advection near the frontal boundary. As a result, 
rain has blossomed in coverage the past few hours, with enough 
elevated instability for embedded convection as well. Expect this 
area of rain and embedded thunder to continue slowly moving east 
across northern Ohio early this morning, reaching NW PA by about 
11Z. Heavy downpours will occur within any convection in this moist 
environment (PWATs near 2 inches), but progressive movement should 
limit any flooding concerns.

Behind this morning's shortwave, the front will stall west-east 
across the CWA, but confidence is low on exactly how far south it 
will push since another shortwave and an associated weak surface low 
will be approaching for tonight. The presence of the boundary 
overhead, diurnal heating, and the abundant low-level moisture will 
support another round of scattered convection this afternoon and 
evening, but confidence is low on coverage and location since this 
morning's rain and thunder trended higher in coverage. Lingering 
clouds and showers through late this morning may limit diurnal 
heating and keep instability a little weaker for the afternoon. 
Nevertheless, expect at least some afternoon thunderstorms, and the 
lake breeze boundary as well as differential heating boundaries 
farther inland may serve as initiation points depending on the exact 
location of the synoptic front. Locally heavy rainfall possible once 
again wherever any storms can develop.

The next aforementioned mid/upper shortwave looks to progress east 
across the southern Great Lakes and Upper Ohio Valley tonight. This 
will once again have decent mid-level PVA and upper diffluence, and 
with weak instability persisting overnight again, expect showers and 
embedded convection throughout the night to be quite widespread in 
coverage. In fact, coverage tonight may be greater than this 
afternoon due to the forcing moving overhead. A trailing cold front 
behind this wave looks to move through Saturday afternoon and 
overtake the old frontal boundary, effectively pushing everything 
south for a brief period Saturday night and Sunday, but before that 
happens, one last round of scattered convection is expected ahead of 
the front Saturday. Coverage will again be dependent on the amount 
of instability after the overnight/early morning activity. Areas 
that see the most frequent convection between this morning and 
Saturday evening could experience flooding of low-lying, poor 
drainage, and urban areas, as well as rises on area rivers and 
streams since the environment will be conducive to heavy rainfall 
rates (high freezing levels, deep warm cloud layer, PWATs near 2 
inches, and tall, skinny CAPE).

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Weak high pressure will briefly bring dry and less 
humid conditions Saturday night and Sunday, but the front will 
retreat back north as a warm front Sunday night as the high drifts 
east ahead of a potent mid/upper shortwave dropping into the Upper 
Midwest. Scattered convection is possible in the warm air advection 
near the retreating front, but there will also be an MCS ongoing 
upstream over the western Great Lakes driven by a 35-40 knot low-
level jet and strong warm/moist advection. If this MCS can survive 
into our region, then damaging winds and heavy rain are possible 
late Sunday night. The best chance for this would be in NW and north 
central Ohio and the western half of Lake Erie before it outruns the 
best support and instability. 

The strong shortwave will cross the central Great Lakes Monday, with 
a trailing cold front dropping across the region by Monday night. 
Mid-level flow increasing to 40-50+ knots as the shortwave passes 
will support over 40 knots of deep layer effective shear, so 
depending on how overnight convection plays out in terms of clouds 
and outflow boundaries, additional severe convection is possible 
Monday afternoon and evening, possibly in the form of an organized
